texts.exact_text: Hsiâo Kwo indicates that (in the circumstances which it implies) there will be progress and attainment. But it will be advantageous to be firm and correct. (What the name denotes) may be done in small affairs, but not in great affairs. (It is like) the notes that come down from a bird on the wing; -- to descend is better than to ascend. There will (in this way) be great good fortune.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 62; scan-backed transcription p. 201, hexagram statement
texts.notes: Legge's title restored from the source statement.

texts.exact_text: The first SIX, divided, suggests (the idea of) a bird flying, (and ascending) till the issue is evil.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 62; scan-backed transcription p. 201, line 1

texts.exact_text: The second SIX, divided, shows its subject passing by his grandfather, and meeting with his grandmother; not attempting anything against his ruler, but meeting him as his minister. There will be no error.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 62; scan-backed transcription p. 201, line 2

texts.exact_text: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject taking no extraordinary precautions against danger; and some in consequence finding opportunity to assail and injure him. There will be evil.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 62; scan-backed transcription p. 201, line 3

texts.exact_text: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject falling into no error, but meeting (the exigency of his situation), without exceeding (in his natural. course). If he go forward, there will be peril, and he must be cautious. There is no occasion to be using firmness perpetually.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 62; scan-backed transcription p. 201, line 4

texts.exact_text: The fifth SIX, divided, (suggests the idea) of dense clouds, but no rain, coming from our borders in the west. It also (shows) the prince shooting his arrow, and taking the bird in a cave.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 62; scan-backed transcription p. 201, line 5

texts.exact_text: The sixth SIX, divided, shows. its subject not meeting (the exigency of his situation), and exceeding (his proper course). (It suggests the idea of) a bird flying far aloft. There will be evil. The case is what is called one of calamity and self-produced injury.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 62; scan-backed transcription p. 201, line 6

texts.exact_text:
The name Hsiâo Kwo is explained both by reference to the lines of the hexagram, and to the meaning of the characters. The explanation from the lines appears immediately on comparing them with those of Tâ Kwo, the 28th hexagram. There the first and sixth lines are divided, and between are four undivided lines; here the third and fourth lines are undivided, and outside each of them are two divided lines. The undivided or yáng lines are great, the divided or yīn lines are called small. In Hsiâo Kwo the divided or small lines predominate. But this peculiar structure of the figure could be of no interest to the student, if it were not for the meaning of the name, which is small excesses or exceeding in what is small. The author, accepted by us as king Wén, had in his mind our distinction of essentials and non-essentials. Is it ever good to deviate from what is recognised as the established course of procedure? The reply is -- never in the matter of right but in what is conventional and ceremonial -- in what is nonessential -- the deviation may be made, and will be productive of good. The form may be given up, but not the substance. But the thing must be done very carefully, -- humbly and reverently, and in small matters.

The symbolism of the bird is rather obscure. The whole of it is intended to teach humility. It is better for the bird to descend, keeping near to where it can perch and rest, than to hold on ascending into the homeless regions of the air.

Line 1 is weak, in an odd place, and possessed by the idea of exceeding, which belongs to the hexagram. Its correlate is the strong 4, belonging to the trigram ☳ Zhèn, the attribute of which is movement. There is nothing to repress the tendency of 1; rather it is stimulated; and hence the symbolism.

Line 2 is weak, but in its proper place, and in the centre. Its correlate is 5, which is also a weak line.

The lines 3 and 4 between them are both strong; and are supposed to represent the father and grandfather of the subject of 2; but he or she goes past them, and meets with the grandmother in 5. Again, 5 is the ruler's seat. The subject of 2 moves on to him, but not as an enemy; but humbly and loyally, as his minister according to the attributes of a weak line in the central place. It must be allowed that this view of the symbolism and its interpretation is obscure and strained.

The subject of line 3 is too confident in his own strength, and too defiant of the weak and small enemies that seek his hurt.

Line 4 is also strong, but the exercise of his strength by its subject is tempered by the position in an even place. He is warned, however, to continue quiet and restrain himself.

Line 5, though in the ruler's seat, is weak, and incapable of doing anything great. Its subject is called king or duke because of the ruler's seat; and the one whom in the concluding sentence he is said to capture is supposed to be the subject of 2.

The first part of the symbolism is the same as that of the Tuàn under hexagram 9 ䷈, q.v. I said there that it probably gave a testimony of the merit of the house of Zhōu, as deserving the throne rather than the kings of Shāng. That was because the Tuàn contained the sentiments of Wén, while he was yet only lord of Zhōu. But the symbolism here was the work of the duke of Zhōu, after his brother king Wǔ had obtained the throne. How did the symbolism then occur to him? May we not conclude that at least the Xiàng of this hexagram was written during the troubled period of his regency, after the accession of Wǔ's son, king Kāng?

The Kāng Xī editors find in the concluding symbolism an incentive to humility: -- 'The duke, leaving birds on the wing, is content to use his arrows against those in a cave!'

Line 6 is weak, and is at the top of the trigram of movement ☳. He is possessed by the idea of the hexagram in an extreme degree, and is incapable of keeping himself under restraint. 小过 ䷽
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 62; scan-backed transcription p. 201, notes

texts.exact_text: 小過：亨。利貞。可小事，不可大事。飛鳥遺之音，不宜上宜下，大吉。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 易經卦辭

texts.exact_text: 小過，小者過而亨也。過以利貞，與時行也。柔得中，是以小事吉也。剛失位而不中，是以不可大事也。有飛鳥之象焉，有飛鳥遺之音，不宜上宜下，大吉；上逆而下順也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 彖

texts.exact_text: 山上有雷，小過；君子以行過乎恭，喪過乎哀，用過乎儉。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 大象

texts.exact_text: 初六：飛鳥以凶。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 爻 1

texts.exact_text: 飛鳥以凶，不可如何也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 小象 1

texts.exact_text: 六二：過其祖，遇其妣；不及其君，遇其臣；无咎。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 爻 2

texts.exact_text: 不及其君，臣不可過也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 小象 2

texts.exact_text: 九三：弗過防之，從或戕之，凶。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 爻 3

texts.exact_text: 從或戕之，凶如何也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 小象 3

texts.exact_text: 九四：无咎，弗過遇之。往厲必戒，勿用永貞。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 爻 4

texts.exact_text: 弗過遇之，位不當也。往厲必戒，終不可長也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 小象 4

texts.exact_text: 六五：密云不雨，自我西郊，公弋取彼在穴。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 爻 5

texts.exact_text: 密云不雨，已上也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 小象 5

texts.exact_text: 上六：弗遇過之，飛鳥離之，凶，是謂災眚。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 爻 6

texts.exact_text: 弗遇過之，已亢也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/小過; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 62, 小象 6

texts.exact_text:
In Hsiâo Kwo (we see) the small (lines) exceeding the others, and (giving the intimation of) progress and attainment.

Such 'exceeding, in order to its being advantageous, must be associated with firmness and correctness:' -- that is, it must take place (only) according to (the requirements of) the time.

The weak (lines) are in the central places, and hence (it is said that what the name denotes) may be done in small affairs, and there will be good fortune.

Of the strong (lines one) is not in its proper place, and (the other) is not central, hence it is said that (what the name denotes) 'should not be done in great affairs.'

(In the hexagram) we have 'the symbol of a bird on the wing, and of the notes that come down from such a bird, for which it is better to descend than to ascend, thereby leading to great good fortune:' -- to ascend is contrary to what is reasonable in the case, while to descend is natural and right.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix I, Hexagram 62, p. 265

texts.exact_text: (The trigram ☶ representing) a hill and ☳ that for thunder above it form Hsiâo Kwo. The superior man, in accordance with this, in his conduct exceeds in humility, in mourning exceeds in sorrow, and in his expenditure exceeds in economy.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 62, p. 345

texts.exact_text: 'There is a bird flying (and ascending) till the result is evil:' -- nothing can be done to avoid this issue.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 62, line 1, p. 345

texts.exact_text: 'He does not attempt to reach his ruler:' -- a minister should not overpass the distance (between his ruler and himself).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 62, line 2, p. 345

texts.exact_text: 'Some in consequence find opportunity to assail and injure him. There will be evil:' -- how great will it be!
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 62, line 3, p. 345

texts.exact_text: 'He meets the exigency (of his situation), without exceeding (the proper course):' -- (he does so), the position being inappropriate (for a strong line).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 62, line 4, p. 345

texts.exact_text: 'There are dense clouds, but no rain:' -- (the line) is in too high a place.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 62, line 5, p. 345

texts.exact_text: 'He does not meet the exigency (of his situation), and exceeds (his proper course):' -- (the position indicates) the habit of domineering.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 62, line 6, p. 345
